title: Breads and Bread Rolls
summary: Bread is a dough of wheat flour and water, seasoned with a little salt, raised by the action of yeast and then baked in an oven. The four essential ingredients are flour, yeast, water and salt; sugar, fat and eggs are often added for nutritional value, better flavour, colour and texture. Bread is made by fermentation, a process in which yeast, a one-cell plant, feeds on sugar and converts it into carbon dioxide gas, water and alcohol. The sugar comes from the flour itself (about 1%) and any sugar added. The gluten of flour, formed from the proteins of flour on addition of water and salt, gives the dough elasticity or stretchability; kneading develops the gluten. Wheat with a higher percentage of protein is more suitable as it develops stronger gluten. Fresh yeast gives better results; dry yeast is used in 50-70% of the quantity and must be activated in lukewarm water (if no bubbles appear even after half an hour, the yeast is dead). Sugar aids rising of the dough while salt retards or controls gas formation; with too little or no salt the dough rises very quickly and the bread is of poor quality. The liquid used is milk or water; it dissolves salt, sugar and yeast and hydrates the flour. Eggs add colour and flavour, emulsify fats and increase protein. Solid shortenings (butter, margarine, vanaspati) act as tenderizers. The right dough temperature is 27 C (80 F). Proving chambers have controlled temperature and humidity.

Dough: a mixture of flour and liquid made into a stiff paste. Mixing: adding the liquid slowly to the dry ingredients until a dough is formed. Kneading: folding and pushing the dough to develop the gluten so that it becomes smooth, elastic and no longer sticky; do not add more flour to a sticky dough as it makes the bread hard and tough. Fermentation: yeast feeds on sugar and produces carbon dioxide gas and alcohol; carbon dioxide raises the volume and alcohol gives a peculiar flavour; the ideal temperature is 78-80 F (25-30 C). Rising: the dough doubles in volume, kept in a lightly oiled bowl covered with a moist duster. Knocking back: punching the risen dough to deflate it and then kneading until firm, so that air bubbles are distributed and large holes do not form. Proving (proofing): after shaping, the dough is left to rise again until double in size, light and puffy. Glazing: coating rolls or buns before baking with milk (slightly crusty, shiny finish), egg (golden, soft finish) or flour (soft finish) applied with a pastry brush.

Bread rolls are eaten with continental meals; shapes include a simple round, single knot, double knot, clover leaf, coil or turban and plait. Other products are hamburger rolls, fruit buns, bread loaf (about 20 steps; the lid of the tin is greased and tight fitting; baked bread springs back when pressed), milk bread (denser with fewer holes but stays soft longer because it retains moisture) and brown bread (equal quantities of white and whole meal flour; nutritionally superior as whole meal flour is richer in B-complex vitamins and minerals).

External characteristics: volume (neither too big nor too small for its weight), symmetry of shape, bloom and crust colour (a pleasant, even golden brown obtained by caramelization of sugar), evenness of bake and oven spring (expansion of bread volume after it is put in the oven). Internal characteristics: colour, structure, flavour and aroma and moistness (influenced by the condition of gluten and starch; salt, sugar and fat help retain moisture).

Too small a volume: too tight a dough, too little yeast, too little fermentation time, too cold a dough, excess salt or too high oven temperature. Excessive volume: too slack a dough, lack of salt, excess yeast or too much proving time. Pale crust: excessive fermentation, lack of salt, too high dough temperature or excess yeast; too dark reddish brown crust: too much salt, too cold dough or too tight a dough. Cracks: under fermentation, under proofing or oven temperature too high. Sticky crumb: excessive humidity or underbaking. Rapid staling: baking in a cool oven for a longer time, too high dough temperature or too tight a dough. The two diseases of bread are rope and mould, prevalent in warm and humid weather. Rope is caused by the bacterium Bacillus mesentericus vulgatus from improperly washed wheat or unhygienic conditions; bread gets a sickening sweet smell, becomes discoloured and sticky and shows thread-like strands. It is prevented by acidity (acetic acid, calcium propionate at 0.1%), utmost hygiene, proper proving and baking and cooling. Mould spores enter through cracks; white mould is due to Mucor, greenish or bluish to Penicillium and black to Aspergillus niger; prevention is cleanliness, good ventilation, avoiding warm and humid conditions, thorough cooling and increasing the acidity of dough.

False. Flour is the main ingredient by weight.
Fats in bread dough act as tenderizers.

True. The four essential ingredients are flour, yeast, water and salt.

False. It should be a pleasant golden brown.

sa: Explain any 5 characteristics of a good bread.

(i) Volume: neither too big nor too small for its weight. (ii) Symmetry of shape. (iii) Bloom and an even golden brown crust colour. (iv) Evenness of bake and good oven spring. (v) Internal characteristics: pleasant colour, uniform structure with right sized holes, good flavour and aroma, and proper moistness.
List any 5 terms used in bread making.

(i) Dough: a mixture of flour and liquid made into a stiff paste. (ii) Kneading: working the dough to develop gluten. (iii) Fermentation: yeast feeds on sugar and gives carbon dioxide and alcohol. (iv) Knocking back: punching the risen dough to deflate it. (v) Proving and glazing: the second rising after shaping, and brushing a finish of milk, egg or flour before baking.
Discuss any one bread disease and its prevention.

(i) Rope is caused by the bacterium Bacillus mesentericus vulgatus from improperly washed wheat or an unhygienic bakery. (ii) The bread gets a sickening sweet smell, becomes discoloured and sticky and shows thread-like strands. (iii) Prevent it by an acidic medium: acetic acid at 1% of flour or calcium propionate at 0.1%. (iv) Maintain utmost hygiene of equipment, utensils and premises. (v) Prove, bake and cool the bread properly.
Mention any three internal characteristics of bread to judge its quality.

(i) Internal colour is influenced by the type and quality of flour; a proper crumb structure reflects light. (ii) Structure: gas cells of the right size and evenly distributed, as per the formula of the bread. (iii) Flavour and aroma and moistness: under-fermented bread lacks aroma, over-fermented bread is sourish; stale bread is dry.
What are the common faults in bread and their causes? Give any three.

(i) Too small a volume: too tight a dough, too little yeast, too little fermentation time or excess salt. (ii) Pale crust colour: excessive fermentation time, lack of salt, too high a dough temperature or excess yeast. (iii) Cracks in buns and rolls: under fermentation, under proofing or too high an oven temperature.
Distinguish between fresh yeast and dry yeast use in bread making and explain how dry yeast is activated.

(i) Fresh compressed yeast gives better results than dry yeast. (ii) Dry yeast is used in 50-70% of the quantity of fresh yeast as it is more concentrated. (iii) To activate it, dissolve it in a little lukewarm water and add some flour to get a thin paste. (iv) Keep it in a warm place for 10-15 minutes; air bubbles show that it is ready. (v) If no bubbles are seen even after half an hour, the yeast is dead and should not be used.
